title: Context clues for unknown words
blurb: Work out any unfamiliar word from the sentence around it using the six context-clue types and the substitution check.
question: “Unlike his garrulous roommate, who could talk for hours about anything, Mateo rarely spoke at meals.” You have never seen the word “garrulous.” How can the sentence itself tell you what it means, and how do you avoid the trap answer?

teach.body: Context clues are the hints in the words, phrases and sentences around an unfamiliar word that reveal its meaning. On the TEAS, the question “As used in the passage, the word ___ most nearly means...” is never testing whether you already know the word. It is testing whether you can read the clues. Plain English: cover the word, read around it, and the passage tells you what belongs in the gap.

head: Clue type
Signal words
Example
rows: is, means, or, that is, in other words, commas
such as, including, for example, like
because, since, therefore, as a result
the overall meaning of the passage
teach.caption: Appositives (a phrase set off by commas, dashes or parentheses) count as definition clues.

teach.h: Let the signal word choose the clue

root.label: Find the signal near the word

teach.caption: No signal word? Use a synonym nearby or the general sense of the whole passage.

teach.h: Scenario: Priya reads a patient leaflet
teach.body: Priya, a nursing applicant, practices on this leaflet: “After hip surgery, patients are encouraged to become ambulatory, or able to walk on their own, as soon as their surgeon allows. Unlike sedentary patients, who spend most of the day in a bed or chair, early walkers build strength faster. Because the old hallway floors were slick and uneven, walking there was precarious, so the unit installed new flooring and railings. Simple aids, such as walkers, canes and grab bars, are available on every floor.”

items: “Ambulatory”: the signal “or” introduces a restatement. Meaning: able to walk on their own.
“Sedentary”: “Unlike” sets up a contrast with “early walkers,” and the leaflet explains: in a bed or chair. Meaning: inactive, sitting most of the time.
“Precarious”: “Because... slick and uneven” is the cause; installing railings is the effect. Meaning: unsafe, likely to cause a fall.
“Aids”: “such as walkers, canes and grab bars” gives examples. What they share: they help someone move safely. Meaning: helpful devices.

teach.body: Before you look at the options, cover the word and put your own simple word in the gap. Then substitute each option into the sentence and reread. The right answer keeps the sentence's meaning AND its tone. If an option makes the sentence contradict itself (“Unlike his talkative roommate, Mateo was talkative”), it is wrong, however good it sounds.

steps.label: Cover the word
steps.sub: do not guess from its look

steps.label: Substitute
steps.sub: try each option in the gap

head: Trap
What it looks like
rows: The word's everyday sense, not this sentence's
Meaning of a similar word: eminent vs imminent
A synonym of a word next to the target
The trait of the person being contrasted
teach.caption: Trap answers are often real meanings of real words. That is why substitution, not familiarity, decides.

teach.text: In a contrast clue the meaning is the OPPOSITE of the nearby description. In “Unlike his garrulous roommate, Mateo rarely spoke,” the word “quiet” describes Mateo, not the roommate. The TEAS loves to offer “quiet” as a choice. Garrulous means talkative.

items: Six clue types: definition, synonym, antonym/contrast, example, cause and effect, general sense.
Signal words point to the clue type: or/that is, but/unlike, such as, because.
Predict your own word first, then substitute each option.
The right answer keeps both meaning and tone.
Traps: common meaning, look-alike words, nearby words, contrast flips.

summary: You can now decode an unfamiliar word using definition, synonym, contrast, example, cause-and-effect and general-sense clues. You can also confirm your answer by substitution while avoiding the common-meaning, look-alike, nearby-word and contrast-flip traps.

A.q: “After the treadmill test, the nurse noted that the patient was diaphoretic, that is, sweating heavily, and offered him a towel and water.” As used in the sentence, diaphoretic most nearly means
A.why: “That is” signals a restatement: the sentence defines the word as “sweating heavily,” and the towel fits that meaning.

whyNot.0: Breathlessness is a plausible effect of a treadmill test, but the sentence restates the word as sweating.
whyNot.2: Light-headedness is not mentioned; this relies on outside guessing rather than the clue.
whyNot.3: A fever can cause sweating, but the restatement names the sweating itself, not a raised temperature.

A.q: “Unlike her reticent coworker, who seldom shared an opinion in meetings, Dana spoke up at every staff huddle.” As used in the sentence, reticent most nearly means
A.why: “Unlike” contrasts the coworker with Dana, who spoke up every time, and the clause “who seldom shared an opinion” describes the coworker directly. Reticent means reserved.

whyNot.0: Outspoken describes Dana, the person being contrasted with the coworker. This is the contrast-flip trap.
whyNot.1: Nothing in the sentence refers to how long the coworker has worked there.
whyNot.3: The coworker stays quiet; nothing suggests irritation or restlessness.

A.q: “The clinic keeps several analgesics, such as acetaminophen, ibuprofen and aspirin, on hand for patients who arrive with headaches or sore joints.” Based on the context, analgesics are
A.why: The examples (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, aspirin) and their use for headaches and sore joints point to one shared feature: they relieve pain.

whyNot.0: The sentence describes headaches and sore joints, not infections.
whyNot.1: Nothing in the sentence connects these items to sleep.
whyNot.2: The examples are given for symptoms, and none is described as a nutrient.

B.q: “Because the old wooden footbridge had become dilapidated after decades of storms, rangers closed it until crews could replace its rotted planks and rusted bolts.” As used in the sentence, dilapidated most nearly means
B.why: This is a cause-and-effect clue: decades of storms left rotted planks and rusted bolts, so rangers closed the bridge. Dilapidated means fallen into disrepair.

whyNot.1: Crowding would not explain rotted planks or the need for repairs.
whyNot.2: The bridge is closed until crews CAN replace its planks, so it has not been rebuilt.
whyNot.3: Signage problems do not match rotted planks and rusted bolts.

B.q: “The new director was admired for her candor. Staff appreciated her frankness, even when her honest feedback stung.” As used in the passage, candor most nearly means
B.why: The next sentence restates the idea with the synonyms “frankness” and “honest.” Candor means openness or honesty.

whyNot.0: Being a director gives her authority, but the passage praises how she communicates, not her rank.
whyNot.2: Feedback that “stung” suggests honesty rather than kindness.
whyNot.3: “Feedback” is a nearby word, not a synonym for the target. This is the nearby-word trap.

B.q: “The committee's vote was imminent; members had already taken their seats and expected to decide within the hour.” As used in the sentence, imminent most nearly means
B.why: Members are seated and expect to decide within the hour, so the vote is about to happen.

whyNot.0: This is the meaning of the look-alike word “eminent,” not “imminent.”
whyNot.1: A vote expected within the hour is the opposite of postponed.
whyNot.3: The sentence gives no sign of argument; it is about timing.

C.q: “In the early 1900s, the town's water came from shallow wells near livestock pens, and outbreaks of illness were common. After engineers built a filtration plant in 1912, the number of cases fell sharply. City records credit the plant with ameliorating conditions that had troubled residents for decades.” As used in the passage, ameliorating most nearly means
C.why: The general sense of the passage shows that cases fell sharply after the plant opened, so the plant made conditions better. Ameliorating means improving.

whyNot.0: “Recording” echoes the nearby phrase “city records,” not the word being defined.
whyNot.1: This is the opposite: illness decreased after the plant was built.
whyNot.2: Engineers built a plant to fix the problem; the passage does not describe a study of it.

C.q: “Many of the hospital's longtime volunteers are octogenarians; in other words, they are in their eighties.” Which type of context clue helps the reader understand octogenarians?
C.why: “In other words” is a definition/restatement signal: the sentence directly restates the term as people in their eighties.

whyNot.0: There is no contrast word such as “but” or “unlike,” and no opposite is described.
whyNot.1: No list introduced by “such as” or “including” appears.
whyNot.2: No “because” or “therefore” links a cause to a result.

C.q: “Even her opponents admitted that the senator's trenchant questions had exposed the plan's weaknesses with precision. Within a week, the plan was withdrawn.” As used in the passage, trenchant most nearly means
C.why: The questions exposed weaknesses “with precision” and led to the plan's withdrawal, so they were sharp and effective.

whyNot.1: Nothing describes the questions' volume or emotion; the clue is precision.
whyNot.2: Vague questions could not expose weaknesses “with precision.”
whyNot.3: Rambling is the opposite of precise.

reteach.title: Fill in the smudged word
reteach.question: A coffee spill has smudged one word on a note from your roommate: “I'm ______ tonight, so please don't wake me before 6 a.m.” You know what the word must be without seeing it. That instinct is context-clue reading.

blocks.body: You filled the smudge with “exhausted” or “working late” because the rest of the note left only a few possibilities. An unfamiliar word on the TEAS is just a smudge you can see: “I'm somnolent tonight, so please don't wake me.” Treat it as blank, use the surrounding words to predict, and then pick the option that fits the gap. Somnolent means sleepy.

steps.label: Match an option
steps.sub: the one that fits the gap

blocks.text: Do not let a word's look decide. “Somnolent” looks like “solemn,” but substitution shows only “sleepy” fits the note.

explain.body: A definition clue states the meaning, often after “or,” “that is,” “means” or between commas. A synonym clue places a word with a similar meaning nearby, often signaled by “also,” “likewise” or “similarly.”

test.q: “The guide called the cave system labyrinthine; likewise, the tunnels beneath the old hospital formed a maze of twisting passages.” As used in the sentence, labyrinthine most nearly means
test.why: “Likewise” signals a synonym clue: the tunnels are similarly “a maze of twisting passages.” Labyrinthine means complex and winding.

whyNot.0: Caves are often dark and damp, but the clue describes a maze, not moisture or light.
whyNot.1: “Old hospital” describes the building's age, not the meaning of the target word.
whyNot.3: The clue describes twisting, not narrowness or slope.

explain.body: A contrast clue sets the unknown word against its opposite, signaled by “but,” “however,” “unlike,” “whereas” or “instead.” Find the opposite, then flip it.

steps.label: Read the other side
steps.sub: said it in half the words

test.q: “Whereas the first draft of the safety report was verbose, the final version said the same thing in half the words.” As used in the sentence, verbose most nearly means
test.why: “Whereas” sets up a contrast with a version that said the same thing in half the words, so the first draft was wordy.

whyNot.0: This describes the final version, the opposite side of the contrast.
whyNot.1: The contrast is about length, not accuracy.
whyNot.2: Wordy writing can be hard to follow, but the clue contrasts the number of words.

explain.body: Example clues list instances after “such as,” “including” or “for example”: ask what the items have in common. Cause-and-effect clues (“because,” “since,” “as a result”) reveal the meaning through what caused something or what it led to.

test.q: “Ella collects ephemera, including ticket stubs, postcards and newspaper clippings that most people throw away within days.” As used in the sentence, ephemera most nearly means
options: printed items not meant to last
test.why: The examples share two features: they are printed paper and people discard them quickly. Ephemera are printed items not meant to last.

whyNot.0: Furniture is not printed and does not match tickets or clippings.
whyNot.2: Coins are metal and are not thrown away within days.
whyNot.3: Letters from famous people are kept, not thrown away within days.

explain.body: Put each option into the sentence in place of the word. The right answer keeps the meaning and tone. Wrong answers often make the sentence contradict its own clue.

head: Option in the gap
Result
rows: pain came and went: off and on

test.q: “The patient's symptoms were intermittent: the pain came and went over several days.” As used in the sentence, intermittent most nearly means
test.why: The colon introduces a restatement: the pain “came and went.” Substituting “occurring off and on” keeps that meaning.

whyNot.1: The sentence describes a pattern of stopping and starting, not a steady change.
whyNot.2: Constant pain is the opposite of pain that came and went.
whyNot.3: The clue describes timing, not intensity.
